YC’s Fall 2026 batch is out.

I went through every company in it.

Here are 15 B2B startups solving problems most people don’t know exist:

RunInfra (Jaber Jaber, Osama Jaber): Chat prompt → optimised open-source AI inference pipeline. Infra teams skip weeks of setup.

GodHands: Deterministic execution for agents on browsers and desktops. Getting an agent to do the same thing twice is the hard part.

Simantic (Seungmin Hong, Ahnaf Shahriar): Simulated hardware for embedded firmware QA. No more waiting on boards to test.

Collar AI (Kazel Koh En Yang, Jamie Yau): Automates pre-investment work for private market investors. Diligence still lives in spreadsheets.

Qokedas (Wilhelm Hedenskog, Jesper Johansson, Elias Reinfeldt): Turns scientific instrument signals into AI training data. Lab data is the next goldmine.

Forward (Daniel Yoon, Riley Janjis, Darryl Luo): Packages borrower financials into deal materials for private credit funds. Niche buyer, very real pain.

Herdr (Can Celik): Keeps AI coding agent sessions alive in the terminal. Anyone who’s lost a long agent run gets it.
Vorelios (Daniel McNeil, Krish Kapadia): Physics foundation models for engineering simulation.

Hours of simulation → minutes.
Simulithic (Ryan Ning, Satyam Singh): Simulated user cohorts that predict how a product change lands before you ship it.

Lightfield (Luke Mainwaring, Luke Wagner): AI intake and triage for in-house legal teams. Legal’s inbox finally gets an owner.

Lantern (Thomas Chan, Justin Wang-Lap Tang): An AI hiring manager for sourcing, interviews and screening.

Workers IO (Chaitanya Choudhary): Virtual environments that reproduce hard-to-find bugs.

“Works on my machine” finally has an answer.
Nodus (Viswa Kotra, Pranav Varshney): Runs AI workloads to completion within a set budget. Cost control is the next AI infra fight.

Maritime (Maria Gorskikh, Aryaman Shrivastava): Every AI agent gets its own isolated micro-VM.

Ascii (Anicet Nougaret, Kirill Makarov): Persistent full-VM sandboxes for AI agents.

The pattern I kept seeing: 1 in 3 is building infrastructure for AI agents, not the agents themselves.

Agents get the headlines. Picks and shovels get the contracts.

Using AI on a bid is allowed. Answers nobody checked are what lose the marks.
7 signs an evaluator spots, and the fix for each.

UK guidance for public buyers says bidders can use AI, much like hiring a bid writer. It also tells buyers to verify accuracy rather than assume it. So the claims in your answers are more likely to be tested at clarification or presentation.

The answers that get caught tend to look alike. They answer a nearby question, carry no names or numbers, and open the same way as the answer before. An evaluator reading six of them in a row notices quickly.

What fixes it is a short check before anything goes in:

1. Answer the question that was asked
→ Use its wording and answer its parts in order

2. Put one real example in each answer
→ Client, year and result

3. Back every claim with evidence you could show
→ If you couldn't show it at clarification, cut it

4. Open with the answer
→ Proof second, company background last

5. Make the risks specific to this contract
→ Name the risk and the person who owns it

6. Read it aloud
→ Cut the words your team wouldn't say in a meeting

7. Check promises against the price
→ Each commitment needs a line in the pricing schedule

Twenty minutes per answer is a lot less than losing a 20% question because the evaluator stopped trusting it.

Which of the seven do you see most often in reviews?

Repost this for a bid team using AI on a live tender.

Raspond drafts first answers from your own approved responses, with real clients, dates and results already in them, so the check is about judgment rather than starting over. Built by people who've led it.

I started my HR career in the 1990s overseeing HRIS systems and implementation, when “technology in HR” meant payroll systems and databases. Over 30 years I’ve learned one thing about technology: it scales what we feed it.

AI learns from our hiring history, and that history isn’t neutral. About 40% of applications are now screened out by AI before a person ever sees them. Meanwhile, 68% of recruiters believe AI removes bias. The evidence doesn’t support that.

Think about who gets filtered out quietly: the racialized candidate, the woman in a role most exposed to disruption, and the person with a resume gap because they were incarcerated. My years as a board chair and volunteer mediator in community justice taught me how much a second chance depends on someone opening the door. An algorithm trained on “who we hired before” will keep that door shut.

A record should not last a lifetime. Neither should a biased data pattern.
HR has to move from awareness to governance:
🔹 Treat AI-assisted decisions as employment decisions. Accountability stays with us, not the vendor.
🔹 Require independent bias audits, and actually read the results.
🔹 Keep humans in the loop, and be able to explain overrides.
🔹 Write fairness into RFPs, renewals and vendor contracts. No black boxes.
This is what moving from allyship to advocacy looks like in practice.

Most tech workers no longer work at tech companies. That is the finding buried in Motion Recruitment's 2027 Tech Salary Guide. Only about 40% of technical professionals work for technology firms. Healthcare, manufacturing, government, and financial services employ the majority, and those sectors are where hiring signals are now strongest.

A survey released by Express Employment Professionals puts the other side of the picture in focus. Seventy-one percent of U.S. companies are now actively building contract workers into their staffing strategies. 

The percentage of hiring managers planning to engage temporary or contract workers increased significantly, rising from 16% in spring 2025 to 25% in fall 2026, a 9-percentage-point increase, signaling growing demand for flexible workforce solutions. 

Non-tech industries competing for technical talent are turning to the contingent channel. The economics work. The speed works. The flexibility works, especially for organizations that need AI, cybersecurity, or data capabilities without the overhead of a permanent hire.

The salary guide also surfaces something interesting. Fifty-five percent of employers now say they regret decisions tied to AI-related layoffs. Only 10% are cutting headcount because of AI. The majority, 39%, are redistributing tasks. The workforce calculus is being recalibrated in real time.

A 2024 systematic review by Souza and colleagues, published in MDPI's Administrative Sciences, examined how businesses across healthcare, manufacturing, education, and finance are integrating AI into their workforces. The consistent finding across 20 studies: the shortage of skilled professionals in AI is real, it is cross-sectoral, and organizations that adapt their skill strategies continuously outperform those waiting for the market to stabilize.

The market has already moved. The question for program leaders is whether your supplier network reflects where technical talent demand is living now.

It’s been 5 weeks since I left my last role.
 
If you’ve had unexpected news recently, or you’ve been searching for a while, this is for you. Keep pressing on.
 
The market is interesting right now. There are plenty of opportunities, but what I’ve learned is that businesses look for one of two people: someone with experience in their exact sector, or someone with the right attitude, who listens, learns and wants to be coached. In my view, you can teach experience, but you can’t teach attitude. The word I hear most about myself is resilience, and being comfortable when things are unclear.
 
What’s worked for me:
 
→ It’s a numbers game. Put in the work and hunt down the roles you actually want.

→ Network as much as you send CVs. If a role interests you, message the line manager or someone on the team. Some won’t reply, because they want to keep the process fair, but some will, and it’s great intel.

→ Use everything: LinkedIn, Google, Indeed. You can even set an AI tool to pull a daily list of roles that fit you, though some sites block it.

→ Consider contract work. 3, 6, 9 or 12 months while you look for the right permanent role.
 
In 5 weeks I’ve had many interviews. I’ve also had plenty of “no” replies, usually “too much experience” or “not enough”. It’s frustrating, but it’s part of it.
 
Job hunting is a full-time job, and it’s unpaid. Keep your head up. Christmas is coming, but things still happen.
 
If you want my list of job sites or an introduction to someone, DM me. And if you’re hiring, let me know.

Why are global consultancies buying EdTech platforms while EdTech giants hire Big 4 partners?

Today Ronnie Screwvala announced the launch of upGrad Next - bringing in senior human-capital partners from Deloitte, EY, and Aon - my immediate thought was: this is the reverse Accenture LearnVantage play.

Accenture started in the boardroom and bought Udacity to move downstream into learning.

upGrad started in learning and is hiring org-design and rewards partners to move upstream into the boardroom.

The reason is simple: selling standalone course catalogs in the AI era has hit a wall. As Cognizant’s recent talent architecture blueprint pointed out, there is a 61-point execution gap between what AI can do on paper and what enterprises actually absorb. You can’t close that gap with video licenses if a company’s job families, approval chains, and incentives are still frozen in 2019.

The real leverage today is getting into the room before an enterprise decides it needs training.

But combining advisory and skilling under one roof raises a defining question for the entire industry:

> Can a learning company tell you that training isn’t the answer?

If a workflow is slow because three layers of middle managers duplicate the same review, will an adviser whose parent company runs a massive skilling engine tell you not to buy training? And once the org chart is redrawn, how do you actually verify that people can execute the changed work on Monday morning? (It’s the exact missing-middle problem we spend every day wrestling with at Altiv.AI).

In my latest piece on Edtech B.E.T., I break down:

🔹 Where upGrad Next and Accenture LearnVantage collide in the AI workforce stack
🔹 Why tasks - not job descriptions - are now the only unit of analysis that matters
🔹 The 4-Question Evidence Standard every CHRO and COO should demand before signing an AI transformation contract

Your AI tool keeps rejecting certain job applicants, and nobody on the team can say what it based its decisions on. Is that a technical problem or a legal one?

It can start as a technical problem, but the legal consequences fall on the company. Imagine the tool rejects applicants of one race, or older applicants, more often than others. Nobody meant for that to happen, but laws against discrimination can still apply when software makes the decision. The company using the tool could face legal trouble, and a federal court in California has let claims go forward against one software company in a case that is still ongoing. If nobody can show how the tool reaches its decisions or whether it has been tested for unfair results, defending it can become much harder.

Engineers test whether an AI product works, meaning whether it is secure, accurate and stable. Those tests do not show where the company could get into legal trouble, which takes a different set of questions.

When an AI product is about to go live, these are some of the questions I raise:

-Is it used for something with special rules, like hiring, lending or health?
-Can you explain how it makes decisions, and has it been checked for unfair results?
-Do you have the right to use the data behind it, and do people know how it is used?
-Who is responsible when it gets something wrong, and do your contracts and user terms say so clearly?

Raising these questions early can be easier than fixing them once the product is in use, and it means you have answers ready when customers or regulatory agencies ask.

What's one question you wish your team had asked before launch?

Stoa, a Helsinki-based AI startup, has raised €3.5 million in pre-seed funding led by Lifeline Ventures to bring AI to construction sites and data centers.

The company's platform brings together drawings, schedules, and quality and safety reports, using AI to give teams an up-to-date view of their projects. Lifeline Ventures was joined by Illusian, the investment company associated with Supercell co-founder Ilkka Paananen and Wolt co-founder Miki Kuusi, and Wave Ventures. Angel investors include former Nokia CEO Pekka Lundmark Virala Oy Ab CEO Alexander Ehrnrooth, SRV board member Tuomas Kokkila, and PlanGrid, an Autodesk company co-founders Tracy Young and Ralph Gootee.

Stoa is led by co-founder and CEO Johannes Korpela. Co-founder and Chief Product Officer Taavi Paananen said AI can read drawings, contracts, and building information models to help teams prevent mistakes, while co-founder Camilla Komulainen emphasized that humans remain involved in decisions and every AI-generated answer cites its original source. Co-founders Eino Miettinen, the company's CTO, and Pyry Pohjanoksa, who leads AI development, are also part of the founding team.

According to Komulainen, the platform is already in use at more than 25 Nordic construction sites, including data center projects. The new funding will support further product development, international expansion, and hiring, with a focus on major data center markets in the Nordics, the UK, and the US.

OpenAI and Upwork published numbers on November 10 that say more about hiring than another model launch.

Content writing's share of Upwork postings fell by 31% from the first half of 2025 to the first half of 2026. In the same data, AI-related projects had fixed-price budgets about 52% higher than similar non-AI work in the same category and month. Hired hourly contracts ran about 41% more hours in the first 90 days. Posted hourly rates barely moved, about 1.5%.

Clients are buying bigger projects. The brief now bundles implementation, production and a finished deliverable, and that is where the budget went.

If your offer is one task a chatbot already does, the posting is getting smaller. If you can own the project around that task, the budget is getting larger.

Month 9. Monday morning. The new institute's website stopped loading.
Enquiry forms down. Parent emails bouncing.

The domain had expired on Saturday. Every renewal reminder went to the personal inbox of the staff member who set it up. She had left in month 4.

So the team went looking for everything else that renews.

They found 14 items in year one: 
→ Building lease 
→ Fire safety NOC 
→ Insurance 
→ LMS and email licences 
→ Domain and hosting 
→ Generator and AC maintenance contracts ...and 8 more.

Only 5 had a date written down anywhere. 3 were still in the name of people who had left.

Nobody was careless. Setup months are a blur of approvals, hiring and fit-outs. Papers get signed, filed and forgotten. Until one lapses.

The fix is a setup register, written before opening day:
→ Every licence, approval and contract on one sheet 
→ A renewal date and one named owner for each 
→ A reminder 60 days out, sent to a role inbox, not a person.

That register is part of how we set up new institutes in our New Institutional 
Setup work. Openings get celebrated. Renewals keep the doors open.

Opening an institute this year? List what renews before you cut the ribbon.

My speech for the graduates of 2026:

Good evening game development students, class of 2026, and let me also congratulate you on graduating from Digital Arts and Entertainment.
This speech is difficult for me and I am also nervous, because we must talk about the future. There is an elephant in the room here this evening and it is of course artificial intelligence. I trust that everybody has heard enough about AI the last few weeks and months and is perhaps even sick of it. Social media is full of articles about AI and how it is transforming the workplace. 
But before we hop on the bandwagon perhaps it is appropriate to reflect on the impact AI has on society.
Perhaps it is not a good idea to ditch 60,000 people from your workforce, unless you want your product to be called Microsoft 364.
Perhaps it is not a good idea to hand over critical software over to AI, lest you want to ground your planes for half a day.
Perhaps it is also not a good idea for Belgian schools and universities to fill the coffers of U.S. companies such as Microsoft and OpenAI via public funding which is ultimately paid for by taxpayers. Even more so when the ethics of those companies with regards to the social contract is questionable.
As a coordinator of a small university of a small country, all I can do is raise my voice. But perhaps if enough of use raise our voices we can be heard. 
And it IS important as there is a lot of uncertainty for our freshmen, enrolled students and graduates. It used to be customary that students questioned certain subjects or courses in a study program. But a much more pernicious question is rearing its head: “Why study anything at all? Why practice anything at all ?”  
From our point of view as a technical university we offer formation. We develop skills and knowledge. I would argue that a broad and foundational knowledge is even more important in the current era. My message to students and graduates is clear: domain knowledge and skills ARE important, let nobody tell you otherwise. It may be the case that you arrive at a game studio where the use of AI is permitted, or even obligatory. But the skills you developed here and the knowledge that you have is what will carry your professional life.
There is a saying that it takes a village to raise a child. I carry that over to game development: “It takes a village to create a game”. You need people from all walks of life, of all ages and backgrounds to create a successful game. Not hiring juniors as a shortsighted way to save cost is penny wise and pound foolish. The new generation needs the opportunity to grow by making the mistakes we all made when we started out as professionals.
Players want games created by humans, for humans. We want to hear stories that were written by humans and immerse ourself in fictional worlds that evoke a meaningful experience. I am convinced that this generation of freshly graduated game developers can bring that experience with or without AI.

Call it purpose drift: the tool's stated purpose stays put while its real use moves. Under EU law, for firms within the AI Act's reach, the provider is the party that carries the maker's duties. Article 25 of the AI Act treats a deployer as the provider in three cases. One is when it changes the intended purpose of an AI system, a general-purpose one included, so that it becomes high-risk. Decisions on promotion, task allocation based on individual behaviour and the evaluation of staff performance are on the high-risk list.

The Commission's draft guidelines on classification, issued on 19 May 2026, repeat this warning for deployers. The final version is due by the end of 2026. The AI Omnibus (Regulation 2026/1744) moved the high-risk rules for these uses to 2 December 2027. ONS found 55% of employees in Great Britain using AI for work or education in May and June 2026. Only 35% of UK businesses with 10 or more employees reported AI use. The employee figure may include some AI use outside formal business activities. The Act also adds a catch. Suppose a vendor has clearly said its tool must not become a high-risk system. It then need not hand over the documentation a new provider would need.

Three steps. Ask every AI vendor to state in writing which uses it excludes. Keep a list of what staff really use each tool for, and who decides. Route any use that touches hiring, pay, promotion or task allocation through one named approver. A tool used that way needs a different contract, not a different prompt.

If nobody can say what staff really use your general AI tools for, we start there.
